name: Daria Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the night-to-morning crew on the injection moulding machines at Brightpack, where we make yoghurt pots and takeaway tubs. I start at 6, check the overnight scrap bin, and then I'm tuning temperatures and cycle times on eight machines, because plastic behaves differently when the weather changes. I love the puzzle of it, but my feet don't love the concrete floor any more.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The retailers, to be honest. Our biggest customer sends a new price cut every year, and then the plant squeezes the floor to find it. I'm a union rep as well, so I spend half my breaks explaining to people why the schedule changed again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, it'll save a few minutes on reports and that's about it. At work I'd tell the crew to keep the free tools for the boring stuff, like drafting an email, and not worry. Online I'd probably keep quiet, because I've seen too many people shout about this stuff without ever running a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd still worry a little, but about the plant, not about AI. We lost a big yoghurt contract two years ago, and it took four months to fill the hole. At 58 with a few years to go, a bad year at Brightpack scares me more than a clever chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and I'd keep using the chatbot to translate the maintenance manuals from the German machine maker, since that saves me an hour a week. I'd put a bit more into the savings account each month, maybe 150. And I'd keep pushing for the fair shift pattern in the union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit relaxed, but with a grumble in the back of my mind. Nothing changes means the pressure from the retailers stays too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How are things at home with money, in a picture where nothing much changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband Neil retired early from the bus depot because of his back, so his pension is small, and my pay carries most of the household. We have about three months in the bank, and our grown-up kids are on their own, mostly. So I can't afford the plant having a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What do you actually use them for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to translate the German manuals and to tidy up my shift notes, since my spelling is dreadful. The chatbot once gave me machine settings that would have burned the mould, so now I only trust it for words.

say: I'd tell the crew to use free AI tools for **boring jobs** like emails and not to worry.
Online I'd stay quiet, because many people shout about this who have never run a **machine**.
think: I worry about the **plant**, not AI, since we lost a big yoghurt contract two years ago.
With a few years left, one bad year at **Brightpack** scares me more than a chatbot.
do: Keep using a chatbot to translate **German manuals**, which saves about an hour a week.
Put roughly **150 a month** extra into savings.
Keep pushing the **fair shift pattern** in union meetings.
feel: **Relaxed** on the surface, with a grumble about retailer pressure in the back of my mind.
S0.quote: The chatbot once gave me machine settings that would have burned the mould, so now I only trust it for words.
fieldNote: **Her worry** is the plant's contracts, not AI, and it's already part of her daily life.
**Steady and practical** about tools: tried one, found its limits, now uses it only for words.
**Household income** rests mostly on her pay, since her husband retired early with a small pension.

steps.text: Keep translating the German maintenance manuals with a chatbot
Keep running the eight machines on the same crew pattern
Press the union for a fair shift pattern

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and I'd say the office goes first. The people who plan orders, check quality reports and handle customer emails will be the ones who see it. On the floor, we'll get more cameras and more sensors, but the machines still need somebody who knows how plastic behaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I think is that I'm in the middle. The thinking work gets taken by software, like scheduling and ordering, so the planners are in trouble, but the robots take longer to come to the floor. I'd be safe for a bit, but my team lead role includes a lot of reporting, and that part could be moved to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the plant to send me on the training for the new monitoring system, since somebody on the floor needs to understand it. I'd also join the union committee talking to management about it. And I'd cut our subscription spending and holiday plans a bit, to push savings up to about five months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. I'm curious, because the systems sound clever, but I don't like people at the plant being treated as a line on a sheet. I'd feel respected if they'd ask us first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your plant makes physical things. What changes first at Brightpack?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing is the planning room, where five people decide what we run. Software could do that in minutes, and they'd keep two. Then the quality checks, where cameras look for flaws and flag them, which I'm fine with since I hate checking pots by eye at 3 in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter Gwen about her teaching job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Gwen that teachers will use this stuff too, and she should learn it before the school forces it on her. She's good at spotting what works. I'd say the human part of her job, keeping 30 teenagers calm, is the part no one can replace.

say: I'd say this is real, and the **office goes first**: planning, quality reports and customer emails.
I'd tell the crew we still need people who know how **plastic behaves**.
think: The planners are in trouble, but robots reach the floor more **slowly**, so I'm safe for a while.
Reporting is a big part of my lead role and could move to **software**.
do: Ask to be sent on the training for the new **monitoring system**.
Join the union committee that talks to management about **automation**.
Cut subscriptions and holiday plans to reach about **five months** of savings.
feel: **Curious** about how clever the systems sound, but uneasy about people becoming a line on a sheet.
I'd feel **respected** if management asked the floor first.
S1.quote: The thinking work gets taken by software, like scheduling and ordering, so the planners are in trouble, but the robots take longer to come to the floor.
fieldNote: **Practical optimism**: she sees which tasks go first and where she sits in that.
**Union habit** shows in her wish to be asked before changes arrive.
**Money** is modest, so even a mild squeeze leads her to save more.

steps.text: Ask to go on the plant's training for the new monitoring system
Join the union committee that meets management about automation
Cancel two subscriptions and skip the summer trip
Build savings up to five months of bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to talk about this right now, not later. A union rep's job in that world is to get the plant, the town and the government in one room, because two years is a blink. I'd be saying it at work, at the union hall, and probably annoying people online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'd be scared, and I'd also be plotting. The planning and checking goes in 2028, and it takes a lot of people with it, including some in my own team. I'd have about three more years on the floor before robots can run a mould like I do, and that's if the plant doesn't go bust first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Neil about our budget that same week and put everything extra into the bank. I'd ask the plant for a place in the first group to learn the new control systems, because if I'm one of the people who runs the robots, I stay. I'd also start a list of what I can do if Brightpack closes, like machine servicing or training younger staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wobbly. Some days I'd be okay and some days I'd be sat in the car outside the plant for ten minutes before I could walk in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about 2031, so about three years after the thinking AI. How does that look for your hands-on job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have until 2031 before robots do my kind of work, so that's the only cushion I have, and it's not much. If I can run and maintain the robots, I have a chance. If I'm just the one who used to do it by hand, I'm gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from government if this happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper income floor, and money for retraining that people can actually get while they're still on a pay cheque. The government should bring the unions and the companies together early, not hand out a leaflet after the plant closes. I'd also want the profit from automation taxed fairly, because it's workers who built that value.

say: I'd say we must talk now, and a union rep should put the **plant, town and government** in one room.
Two years is a **blink**, and I'd say so loudly at work, at the hall and online.
think: Thinking AI takes planning and checking in **2028**, including some jobs in my own team.
I have about **three more years** of hand-on mould work before robots can match me, if the plant survives.
do: Sit down with Neil that week and put every spare pound into the **bank**.
Ask to be in the first group trained on the new **control systems**.
Draw up a list of fallback work, like **machine servicing** and teaching younger staff.
feel: **Wobbly**: some days I'm fine, some days I'd sit in the car ten minutes before going in.
S2.quote: I have until 2031 before robots do my kind of work, so that's the only cushion I have, and it's not much.
fieldNote: **Anxious but active**: her fear turns straight into plans, which keeps her short of alarmed.
**Union instincts** appear again, wanting government and companies to meet early.
**The 2031 gap** gives her a specific window to act in.

steps.text: Put every spare pound into the bank starting that week
Ask for a place in the first group on the new control systems
Train as a machine servicing technician in the evenings
Lobby the union and councillors for early retraining money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is manageable if people act. I'd tell the crew to get ready slowly, learn the tools one step at a time and not wait for Brightpack to hand us a plan. Five years is enough for a good sensible response.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I really think is that it's survivable for me. I'd be 63 when the thinking AI arrives and 66 when robots reach the moulding floor, so I could finish my working life before the worst. But I'd worry about the plant's younger people, who'd have longer to go and much less to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to take every course the plant or the union offers on the new control systems. I'd build up six months of savings and pay down the rest of our car loan. And I'd keep an eye on whether to retire at 62 or 63, depending on how the pension looks by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, definitely, like having time to breathe. I'd probably still have a funny feeling when I walk past the planning office and see fewer desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what could you do that you couldn't in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years I'd have been scrambling. In five I could learn properly, save properly and plan with my husband Neil. I could also train my younger operators myself, so they're ready for the robot age before I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change how you think about retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it might. If the savings look okay and the pension holds, I'd retire at 62 and spend more time with the grandchildren, if there are any by then. If not, I'd stay to 65 and be the one who knows both the old machines and the new ones.

say: I'd tell the crew to learn the tools **step by step** and not wait for a plan from management.
I'd say five years is enough for a **sensible response**.
think: It's survivable for me, because robots would reach the moulding floor when I'm about **66**.
I worry for the **younger operators** who have longer to go and less to fall back on.
do: Take every course on the new **control systems** that the plant or union offers.
Build **six months** of savings and pay down the car loan.
Decide between **retiring at 62** or staying to 65 once the pension picture is clear.
feel: **Calmer**, like I finally have room to breathe.
A funny feeling when I see **fewer desks** in the planning office.
S3.quote: In two years I'd have been scrambling. In five I could learn properly, save properly and plan with my husband Neil.
fieldNote: **Time helps her**: five years turns panic into a learning plan.
**Concern for others**: she keeps returning to younger operators with less cushion.
**Retirement choice** is open and tied to the pension, not to AI alone.

steps.text: Take every control-system course the plant or union offers
Pay off the car loan and reach six months of savings
Decide on retiring at 62 once the pension numbers are clear
Coach younger operators on the new systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best case, and that it's still a mistake to relax. A ten-year warning is only useful if somebody uses it, and in my experience that somebody is the union and the people who show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it's mostly a story about the grandchildren's generation. I'd be retired and fine, I think, and what would worry me is whether the young ones can find a trade that lasts. I'd stay interested, because a plant is my whole life's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, retire around 62 or 63, and use the first years of retirement to volunteer at the technical college teaching moulding basics. I'd keep the union membership and keep pushing for a retraining fund, because ten years goes fast. I'd also keep using the AI tools a bit, so I'm not a stranger to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A little sad, maybe, because the work I'm good at will change shape, but I'd be at peace with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. Would you do anything differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now to teach someone younger what I know about reading a mould. And I'd do my share of the learning on new tools, just so I can tell the crew what's hype and what's useful. Ten years lets me do both without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if people got left behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big retailers and the owners, for squeezing the plants and not putting money into the people. And the government, for sleeping through the warning. Not the engineers who build the systems, they're doing a job.

say: I'd say it's the best case, but **relaxing** would still be a mistake.
A ten-year warning is only useful if the **union** and people who show up use it.
think: For me it's a story about the **grandchildren's generation**, since I'd be retired and fine.
I'd worry whether young people can find a **trade that lasts**.
do: Retire around **62 or 63** and volunteer teaching moulding basics at the technical college.
Keep my **union membership** and push for a retraining fund.
Keep using **AI tools** a little so I'm not a stranger to them.
feel: **Fairly calm**, and at peace with the work changing shape.
A little **sad** that what I'm good at will look different.
S4.quote: A ten-year warning is only useful if somebody uses it, and in my experience that somebody is the union and the people who show up.
fieldNote: **Secure and settled**: the long runway lets her retire before any real threat.
**Blame** falls on retailers, owners and a government that sleeps through warnings.
**Legacy** matters to her, so she wants to pass on mould-reading skills.

steps.text: Teach moulding basics at the technical college
Keep learning chatbot tools for manuals and notes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no space to breathe. What would help is money for retraining that I can actually reach while I'm still earning, plus a plant that talks to the crew before it decides. I'd also want a pension that doesn't punish me for leaving a few years early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The packers and the cleaners would go first and nobody remembers them. A plant isn't only the operators, and I'd want that said.

headlineQuote: The packers and the cleaners would go first and nobody remembers them. A plant isn't only the operators, and I'd want that said.
portrait: **Daria** is a 58-year-old lead operator and union rep on injection moulding machines at a food-packaging plant, a few years from retirement.
She is **open to change**: she tried a chatbot, learned its limits, and uses it for manuals.
Her husband retired early with a small pension, so her pay and about **three months** of savings carry the household.
She turns fear into plans and union action, moving from uneasy to **anxious** only when robots could arrive before she can retire.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because there's no time to retrain or plan with the plant.
whatWouldHelp: **Retraining money** she can reach while still earning, and a plant that talks to the crew first.
